title: Finding the center
hookLine: a four-minute voice note has one real sentence in it; a hymn has one line marked rahao
tomorrow: why do the lines end in little numbers?

cards: A friend sends a four-minute voice note. Traffic, a story about a cousin, a detour about lunch, and somewhere past the three-minute mark, one sentence, quieter than the rest: I'm scared about my mom's test results.
That's the message. Everything else was circling it. A hymn in the Granth can run long too, verse after verse.
So, which line do you read first? Not always the first one. Look for a single word set after one line, like a pin in a map.

teach.b: Rahao is usually read as pause, or stay here. It often sits right after the first verse, and Sikh teachers point to it as the hymn's center: the idea the other verses circle.
In kirtan, it's often the line the singers keep coming back to, like a chorus.

teach.h: FIND IT FIRST, THEN READ OUTWARD.
teach.b: So with a hymn you don't know, find the rahao, then read outward. Here's a hymn of Guru Arjan's from the evening prayers, where that changes everything.

Its opening, in paraphrase: why, mind, do you scheme and worry, when the Lord is already at work for you? Even creatures inside rocks and stones have their food set before them. That's the line people remember.

Now the rahao, in paraphrase: whoever meets the true company is carried across; by the Guru's grace they reach the highest state, and dry wood turns green. Read only the opening and the hymn says: stop worrying.

teach.h: THE CENTER: DRY WOOD TURNS GREEN.
teach.b: Read the center and it says where the worry can go: into good company, under a grace that turns dry wood green. That's something for a hard week, the kind with a hospital appointment on the calendar.
The worry doesn't have to be argued away alone.
The center of the hymn sits you down with other people. And here's a fact for tonight: in the Granth, the line that holds a hymn's meaning is often marked with a word that means pause.

how: Sikh teachers often begin explaining a shabad from its rahao line, and in kirtan the rahao is commonly sung as the refrain the singers return to between verses.

the line marked rahao, then the verses around it.

games.why: the rahao is the hymn's center. in Guru Arjan's hymn the opening asks why worry; the center answers: in true company, dry wood turns green.

practice: Find one hymn, in a gutka or an app, and look for the word rahao. Read that line once, slowly, out loud or under your breath.
Then close your eyes and let it come back to you on each breath out, the way a chorus comes back, until the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Finding the center: going first to the rahao line, the line marked pause, where a hymn's main idea sits, and reading outward from there. The seventh word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rahao, read as pause or stay; it marks a hymn's central line.

carryVoice: The line for today: start at the center, where dry wood turns green. Seven down.
